claim: The human brain is approximately three times larger than would be expected in a primate with the same body mass.
source: It is known that the human brain is approximately three times larger than would be expected in a primate with the same body mass (Rilling, 2006; Rilling, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rilling, 2006 and Rilling, 2014.

claim: A greater proportion of the human brain's cortical surface is allocated to higher-order association cortices compared to primary sensory and motor areas.
source: Beyond general growth, neuroimaging analyses via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have indicated that a greater proportion of the human brain's cortical surface is allocated to higher-order association cortices compared to primary sensory and motor areas (Smaers et al., 2017; Avants et al., 2006; Van Essen and Dierker, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smaers et al., 2017; Avants et al., 2006; and Van Essen and Dierker, 2007.

claim: The expansion of association areas in the human brain is accompanied by increased anatomical connectivity.
source: This expansion of association areas is accompanied by increased anatomical connectivity (Ardesch et al., 2019), providing a structural substrate assumed to enable efficient region-to-region communication and integration of remote neural processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ardesch et al., 2019.

claim: The human connectome shows widespread overlapping topological properties with those of other primates like macaque and chimpanzees.
source: Studies of the brain's structural wiring, known as the human connectome, have shown widespread overlapping topological properties (e.g., small-world and modularity properties; Ardesch et al., 2019) with those of other primates (like macaque and chimpanzees), accompanied by subtle but potentially consequential species differences (van den Heuvel et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ardesch et al., 2019 and van den Heuvel et al., 2016.

claim: Diffusion MRI data were obtained for 58 humans (Homo sapiens, 42.5±9.8 years, female) and 22 chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes, 29.4±12.8 years, female).
source: Diffusion MRI data for 58 humans (H. sapiens, 42.5±9.8 years, female) and 22 chimpanzees (P. troglodytes, 29.4±12.8 years, female) were taken from previous studies (Ardesch et al., 2019; van den Heuvel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with specific numbers and demographic information.

claim: Intrahemispheric pathways comprise 82.6% (19 out of 23) of human-specific connections.
source: We find that intrahemispheric pathways comprise 82.6% (19 out of 23) of human-specific connections and 50% (3 out of 6) of chimpanzee-specific connections, a finding consistent with previous comparative connectome investigations (Ardesch et al., 2019; van den Heuvel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific numerical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intrahemispheric pathways comprise 50% (3 out of 6) of chimpanzee-specific connections.
source: We find that intrahemispheric pathways comprise 82.6% (19 out of 23) of human-specific connections and 50% (3 out of 6) of chimpanzee-specific connections, a finding consistent with previous comparative connectome investigations (Ardesch et al., 2019; van den Heuvel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific numerical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a strong correlation between connectivity strengths of shared connections across both human and chimpanzee species.
source: We also examine the set of connections that are present in both species, termed shared connections (Figure 1C), and confirm that there is a strong correlation between connectivity strengths across both species (Figure 1D), consistent with previous studies (Ardesch et al., 2019; van den Heuvel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing the correlation and citations to previous studies.

claim: The human and chimpanzee connectomes show similar levels of small-worldness with small-world propensity values of 0.83 and 0.84 respectively.
source: In particular, the connectomes show similar levels of small-worldness (small-world propensity [Muldoon et al., 2016] values of 0.83 and 0.84 in human and chimpanzee, respectively) and modularity (modularity values of 0.54 and 0.56 in human and chimpanzee, respectively) (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Rubinov and Sporns, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific numerical values and citations to methodological references.

claim: The human and chimpanzee connectomes show similar levels of modularity with modularity values of 0.54 and 0.56 respectively.
source: In particular, the connectomes show similar levels of small-worldness (small-world propensity [Muldoon et al., 2016] values of 0.83 and 0.84 in human and chimpanzee, respectively) and modularity (modularity values of 0.54 and 0.56 in human and chimpanzee, respectively) (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Rubinov and Sporns, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific numerical values and citations to methodological references.

claim: Human brain regions have significantly shorter path lengths compared to chimpanzee brain regions.
source: On the other hand, human brain regions have significantly shorter path lengths compared to chimpanzee brain regions (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1F showing the data.

claim: The reduced Wong-Wang biophysical model has been shown to reproduce empirical human functional neuroimaging data.
source: This model has been shown to reproduce empirical human functional neuroimaging data (Deco et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019), which we confirmed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to validation data in the manuscript.

claim: The reduced Wong-Wang biophysical model is suitable to match non-human primate data.
source: Notably, we also confirmed the model's suitability to match non-human primate data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to validation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The finding of narrower dynamic range distribution in humans is robust against differences in individual-specific connectomes.
source: This finding is robust against differences in individual-specific connectomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), brain volume (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), connection density (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), inter-individual variability of connection strengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), data sample size (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), propagation delays between brain regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), and heterogeneous excitatory input across brain regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple supplementary figures showing robustness analyses.

claim: The results are replicated on independent human data from the Human Connectome Project.
source: Moreover, our results are replicated on independent human data from the Human Connectome Project (Van Essen et al., 2013; Figure 3—figure supplement 7) and a different computational model (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to replication data and citation to the HCP.

claim: Both human and chimpanzee species follow a dominant gradient of neural dynamic ranges spatially organized along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: When we map the dynamic ranges onto the anatomical locations of each brain region, we find that both species follow a dominant gradient of neural dynamic ranges spatially organized along the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C showing the spatial organization.

claim: Anterior brain regions show neural dynamics with higher dynamic ranges, while posterior regions have lower dynamic ranges.
source: Specifically, anterior brain regions show neural dynamics with higher dynamic ranges, while posterior regions have lower dynamic ranges.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the spatial gradient.

claim: The dominant anterior-posterior gradient is more prominent in chimpanzees than in humans.
source: Interestingly, we observe that this dominant gradient is more prominent in chimpanzees than in humans (Figure 3—figure supplement 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 9A showing the comparison.

claim: Frontal regions are more expanded in humans compared to chimpanzees.
source: A similar anterior-posterior gradient has also been found in empirical evolutionary expansion maps of the human cortex (Wei et al., 2019), with frontal regions being more expanded in humans compared to chimpanzees (Rilling, 2014; Smaers et al., 2017) and the occipital cortex having relatively similar sizes across the two species (Figure 3—figure supplement 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and reference to expansion data.

claim: The occipital cortex has relatively similar sizes across humans and chimpanzees.
source: A similar anterior-posterior gradient has also been found in empirical evolutionary expansion maps of the human cortex (Wei et al., 2019), with frontal regions being more expanded in humans compared to chimpanzees (Rilling, 2014; Smaers et al., 2017) and the occipital cortex having relatively similar sizes across the two species (Figure 3—figure supplement 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to expansion data in Figure 3—figure supplement 9B.

claim: Highly expanded anterior regions have higher dynamic ranges compared to lowly expanded posterior regions in humans.
source: Taken together, we additionally observe that highly expanded anterior regions have higher dynamic ranges compared to lowly expanded posterior regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 9C showing the comparison.

claim: In humans, brain regions belonging to each functional network show relatively similar neural dynamic ranges.
source: In humans, brain regions belonging to each functional network show relatively similar neural dynamic ranges (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing the distribution of dynamic ranges across networks.

claim: In chimpanzees, neural dynamic ranges follow a marked functional hierarchy with cognitive networks having higher median values than sensory networks.
source: Conversely, in chimpanzees, neural dynamic ranges follow a marked functional hierarchy with cognitive networks (i.e., VA, LIM, FP, and DM) having higher median values than sensory networks (i.e., VIS, SM, and DA).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the chimpanzee network hierarchy.

claim: The patterns of within-network changes in functional connectivity versus modulations in global excitability overlap strongly in humans but not in chimpanzees.
source: Furthermore, the patterns of within-network changes in functional connectivity (FC) versus modulations in global excitability overlap strongly in humans but not in chimpanzees (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3E showing the FC patterns.

claim: Similar levels of regional dynamic ranges allow the human brain to better integrate activity within functionally specialized brain networks and the whole brain.
source: Thus, similar levels of regional dynamic ranges allow the human brain to better integrate activity within functionally specialized brain networks (colored lines in Figure 3E) and the whole brain (black line in Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: The finding of better integration in humans is consistent with the higher level of structural integration imposed by the human connectome, as quantified by lower topological path length.
source: This finding is consistent with the higher level of structural integration imposed by the human connectome, as quantified by lower topological path length (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim connects the functional finding to structural data from Figure 1F.

claim: Regions with shorter paths tend to have higher dynamic ranges.
source: Moreover, we find that the heterogeneity in regional path lengths could explain the heterogeneity in neural dynamics, where regions with shorter paths (i.e., lower path length values reflecting higher ability to integrate information between regions) tend to have higher dynamic ranges (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4 showing the relationship.

claim: Regional neural timescales are significantly correlated with dynamic ranges.
source: We find that regional neural timescales (ranges: 0.12–0.24 s for humans and 0.12–0.55 s for chimpanzees) are significantly correlated with dynamic ranges, and this relation is stronger in chimpanzees (Figure 6A; this finding also holds for macaques and marmosets as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6A showing the correlation.

claim: The relation between neural timescales and dynamic ranges is stronger in chimpanzees than in humans.
source: We find that regional neural timescales (ranges: 0.12–0.24 s for humans and 0.12–0.55 s for chimpanzees) are significantly correlated with dynamic ranges, and this relation is stronger in chimpanzees (Figure 6A; this finding also holds for macaques and marmosets as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of correlation strengths in Figure 6A.

claim: At the end of the drift-diffusion simulation, the human brain has a higher accuracy in achieving the correct choice compared to the chimpanzee brain.
source: At the end of our simulation, the human brain has a higher accuracy in achieving the correct choice compared to the chimpanzee brain (Figure 6E; this finding also holds for macaques and marmosets as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6E showing the decision accuracy over time.

claim: The lower early decision accuracy in humans is driven by regions in the chimpanzee brain with low dynamic ranges that can reach correct decisions quickly.
source: This finding is driven by regions in the chimpanzee brain with low dynamic ranges that can reach correct decisions quickly (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6F showing the relationship between dynamic range and accuracy.

claim: Increased excitation leads to faster decision times but poorer overall decision accuracy.
source: We find that increased excitation leads to faster decision times (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B) but poorer overall decision accuracy (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to supplementary figures showing the effects of excitation.

claim: Increased inhibition extends periods of inferior whole-brain decision accuracy of the human brain compared to the chimpanzee brain at earlier times.
source: We also find that increased inhibition extends periods of inferior whole-brain decision accuracy of the human brain compared to the chimpanzee brain at earlier times (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3D showing the effects of inhibition.

claim: T1w:T2w maps have been shown to be a good macroscale proxy of the cortical processing hierarchy in humans and non-human primates.
source: T1w:T2w maps have been shown to be a good macroscale proxy of the cortical processing hierarchy in humans and non-human primates (Hayashi et al., 2021; Glasser et al., 2014; Burt et al., 2018), where unimodal sensory-motor regions tend to be highly myelinated and transmodal regions lightly myelinated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myelination has been found to be tightly coupled with electrophysiological measures of a region's temporal processing speed.
source: Crucially, myelination has been found to be tightly coupled with electrophysiological measures of a region's temporal processing speed (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2020.

claim: T1w:T2w is inversely related to neural dynamic range.
source: Accordingly, we find that T1w:T2w is inversely related to neural dynamic range (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7B showing the relationship.

claim: The human brain has shorter functional paths than the macaque brain.
source: Moreover, the human brain has shorter functional paths (i.e., lower path length values) than the macaque brain (Figure 8B; similar metric used in Figure 1F but applied here on FC matrices), which corresponds to better functional integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8B showing the functional path length comparison.

claim: The human brain has faster timescales than the macaque brain.
source: We also estimated regional timescales by applying the same technique described in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 on fMRI signals, finding that the human brain has faster timescales than the macaque brain (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8C showing the timescale comparison.

claim: Human brain connectivity has evolved to support neural dynamics that maintain relatively high levels of integration between functionally segregated brain systems.
source: Human brain connectivity appears therefore to have evolved to support neural dynamics that maintain relatively high levels of integration between functionally segregated brain systems (Ardesch et al., 2019; van den Heuvel et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the results and supported by citations.

claim: The more heterogeneous distribution of dynamic ranges in chimpanzees supports that diversity in local neural properties is important for rapid computations.
source: This latter result was attributed to the (i) more heterogeneous distribution of dynamic ranges in chimpanzees, supporting that diversity in local neural properties is important for rapid computations (Gollo et al., 2016), and (ii) higher intrinsic levels of inhibition in the human brain (Carland et al., 2015; Lam et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results supported by a citation to Gollo et al., 2016.

claim: Regional diversity and intrinsic inhibition may explain why chimpanzees are able to perform at least as well as, or better than, humans in simple sensory-motor tasks.
source: This regional diversity and intrinsic inhibition may explain why chimpanzees are able to perform at least as well as, or better than, humans in simple sensory-motor tasks (Martin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Martin et al., 2014.

claim: The findings provide a possible neural mechanism for why humans generally outperform chimpanzees in tasks requiring longer computational processing.
source: Moreover, our findings provide a possible neural mechanism for why humans generally outperform chimpanzees in tasks requiring longer computational processing (Tomasello et al., 2005; Thornton et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Tomasello et al., 2005 and Thornton et al., 2012.

claim: Behavioral differences between humans and chimpanzees are more prominent in complex tasks involving intersubjectivity.
source: In line with our results, studies have suggested that behavioral differences between humans and chimpanzees are more prominent in complex tasks involving intersubjectivity (e.g., theory of mind; Herrmann et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Herrmann et al., 2007.

claim: The Default-Mode Network displays significant genetic, anatomical, and functional differences between humans and non-human primates.
source: This important brain capacity is known to be supported by the activity of the Default-Mode Network (DMN) (Buckner et al., 2008; Spreng et al., 2009), which displays significant genetic, anatomical, and functional differences between humans and non-human primates (Wei et al., 2019; Bruner et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The accuracy of the Default-Mode Network for relatively long computations was more accurate in humans compared to chimpanzees.
source: By making use of our simulations assessing decision-making capacity, we found that the accuracy of DMN for relatively long computations was more accurate in humans compared to chimpanzees (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 4 showing the DMN accuracy comparison.

claim: Evolution has shaped the human brain to optimize fast transmodal integration of neural activity across brain regions supporting complex functions including social-cultural skills.
source: Results from the current study suggest that evolution has shaped the human brain to optimize fast transmodal integration of neural activity across brain regions supporting complex functions including social-cultural skills (Margulies et al., 2016; Buckner and Krienen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claim: The evolutionary adaptation of the human brain may hinder rapid processing within functionally specialized systems.
source: While our results are consistent with the hypothesis that the human brain has evolved to facilitate rapid associative computations (Herrmann et al., 2007), they also highlight that this evolutionary adaptation may hinder rapid processing within functionally specialized systems.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results with a citation to Herrmann et al., 2007.

claim: The unique properties of human and chimpanzee brain dynamics may be understood as an evolutionary tradeoff between functional segregation and integration.
source: The unique properties of human and chimpanzee brain dynamics may therefore be understood as an evolutionary tradeoff between functional segregation and integration.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: The anatomical wiring of the human brain distinctly shapes neural dynamics.
source: Here, we combine brain imaging and biophysical modeling to show that the anatomical wiring of the human brain distinctly shapes neural dynamics.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The shaping of neural dynamics in humans is characterized by a narrower distribution of dynamic ranges across brain regions compared with that of chimpanzees.
source: This shaping is characterized by a narrower distribution of dynamic ranges across brain regions compared with that of chimpanzees, our closest living primate relatives.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A narrow dynamic range distribution supports faster integration between regions, particularly in transmodal systems.
source: We find that such a narrow dynamic range distribution supports faster integration between regions, particularly in transmodal systems.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of a key finding supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A broad dynamic range distribution as seen in chimpanzees facilitates brain processes relying more on neural interactions within specialized local brain systems.
source: Conversely, a broad dynamic range distribution as seen in chimpanzees facilitates brain processes relying more on neural interactions within specialized local brain systems.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of a key finding supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human brain dynamics have evolved to foster rapid associative processes in service of complex cognitive functions and behavior.
source: These findings suggest that human brain dynamics have evolved to foster rapid associative processes in service of complex cognitive functions and behavior.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Neuromodulatory agents can modify the biophysical properties of neurons through various cellular mechanisms.
source: In particular, previous work has shown that neuromodulatory agents can modify the biophysical properties of neurons through various cellular mechanisms (Shine et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shine et al., 2021.

claim: One mechanism of neuromodulation is via activation of metabotropic receptors that bring the resting membrane potential of neurons closer to their firing threshold.
source: One mechanism is via activation of metabotropic receptors that bring the resting membrane potential of neurons closer to their firing threshold (Leenders and Sheng, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leenders and Sheng, 2005.

claim: Brain regions with similarly low or high dynamic ranges are more likely to reach equivalent functional states.
source: Brain regions with similarly low or high dynamic ranges are more likely to reach equivalent functional states.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the model behavior described in the text.

claim: The response functions of human brain regions are more similar to one another compared to those of chimpanzees.
source: We find that the response functions of human brain regions (reflecting how activity changes vs. modulations in global excitability) are more similar to one another compared to those of chimpanzees (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A showing the response functions.

claim: The human and chimpanzee connectomes exhibit similar distributions of clustering coefficients.
source: At the regional level, the connectomes exhibit similar distributions of clustering coefficients (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1E showing the distributions.
